#5762. Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF

Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medicare beneficiaries who remain in their current stand-alone Part D drug plans could face sharply higher premiums in 2027 if they don’t switch to lower-cost plans during open enrollment, according to a KFF analysis.

The average monthly premium for stand-alone prescription drug plans, or PDPs, is projected to rise 50%, from $34 in 2026 to $51 in 2027, if current enrollees remain in the same plans, according to the analysis from KFF, an independent source for health policy research, polling and news.

The increase would widen the gap between stand-alone drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans that include prescription drug coverage. KFF projects that drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans that offer Part D coverage, or MA-PDs, will average $9 a month in 2027, compared with $51 for PDPs. The average PDP premium would rise by $17, compared with an increase of less than $2 for MA-PDs.

For Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage, the average beneficiary has 28 Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans (MA-PDs) and 9 stand-alone prescription drug plans (PDPs) to choose from, with varying costs associated with these different options. KFF analysts examined premiums and cost-sharing requirements for Part D coverage in 2027 and how these costs have changed over time, based on Medicare plan landscape and benefits data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

The $51 figure assumes current PDP enrollees remain in their existing plans. The actual average premium could be lower as beneficiaries switch to less expensive plans during open enrollment and new beneficiaries select coverage.

CMS projected a much smaller increase in the national average Part D premium, from $35 to $36. KFF noted that CMS, which based its estimate on September 2026 enrollment, did not explain its calculation methodology.

Among PDP enrollees who do not receive low-income subsidies, 76%, or 10.4 million people, would pay higher premiums if they keep their current plans. About 2.4 million would see their monthly premiums increase by more than $50.

That's a sharp increase from 2026, when only 38,000 enrollees faced monthly premium increases exceeding $50, according to KFF. The Trump administration’s decision to discontinue the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026 ended the additional premium subsidies that were provided to PDP sponsors and the cap on the maximum allowable monthly PDP premium increase, which was set at $50 for 2026, according to KFF analysts.

Another 4.1 million beneficiaries without low-income subsidies are enrolled in zero-premium PDPs this year, but no zero-premium PDPs will be available in 2027.

“With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said in a statement. “There are relatively low-premium PDP options, but people facing large premium increases need to take action if they want to avoid paying significantly more.”

According to KFF's analysis, if PDP enrollees who are not receiving Part D Low-Income Subsidies (LIS) keep their current plan in 2027, more than half (55%), or 7.5 million people, will pay premiums of less than $20 per month, but nearly 30%, or 3.9 million people, will pay at least $100 per month.

Average monthly premiums for the eight national PDPs are projected to range from around $6 to $204 in 2027. Among national PDPs, the two lowest-premium plans are Centene’s Wellcare Value Script Rx, an enhanced PDP with an average premium of $6.50 for 2027, up from $5.80 in 2026,  and Wellcare Classic, a basic PDP with an average premium of $10.90 for 2027, up from $8.60 in 2026, according to the analysis. The national PDPs with the highest average monthly premiums are United’s AARP Medicare Rx Preferred at $204.50, up from $126.00 in 2026, and Humana Premier Rx Plan at $137.40, up from $119.60 in 2026.

The analysis also finds that most Part D enrollees will face a deductible of several hundred dollars for drug coverage in 2027, including 85% of MA-PD enrollees, up from 80% in 2026, and virtually all PDP enrollees, 99.8%, up from 96% in 2026, based on current enrollment. The average Part D deductible in 2027 will be $643 for PDP enrollees, up from $540 in 2026,  and $489 for MA-PD enrollees, rising from $360 in 2026. The standard Part D deductible in 2027 is $700, up from $615 in 2026.

Most Part D enrollees will also face coinsurance rather than fixed copayments for preferred-brand and non-preferred drugs, potentially making their out-of-pocket costs less predictable. Virtually all PDP enrollees will face median coinsurance of 25% for preferred brands and 35% for non-preferred drugs, according to KFF.

#5761. Choosing the Initial Treatment Approach in HER2-Positive Breast Cancer

— "Beyond Diagnosis" continues with Megan Kruse on the myriad of factors that go into that decision

Developed in partnership with the Our Partner

In "Beyond Diagnosis: Early HER2-Positive Breast Cancer," Cleveland Clinic breast oncologist Megan Kruse, MD, and host John Mangels discuss how clinicians can navigate increasingly complex treatment decisions while helping patients understand their diagnosis and care.

Each installment of this series explores key aspects of early HER2-positive breast cancer care, including interpreting pathology, navigating evolving therapies, individualizing treatment, and supporting patients through shared decision-making.

In this second episode, Kruse discusses choosing between upfront surgery and neoadjuvant therapy, balancing treatment efficacy with toxicity, and tailoring treatment decisions to patients' preferences and individual circumstances.

The following is a transcript of their remarks:

Mangels: Welcome to "Beyond Diagnosis," where we talk with doctors about treatment decisions and communicating with patients. I'm your host, John Mangels. HER2-positive breast cancer is a particularly aggressive disease. Targeted therapies are improving patient treatment options, but those advances have also made care more complex.

Today, we'll explore how breast oncologists make clinical decisions, adapt treatment as new information emerges, and help patients understand their choices. Our guest is Dr. Megan Kruse. Dr. Kruse is director of breast medical oncology and co-leader of the breast cancer program at Cleveland Clinic. Dr. Kruse, thanks so much for being here.

Kruse: Thanks for having me. I'm excited about this conversation today.

Mangels: In early-stage disease, a major choice is whether treatment should begin with surgery or systemic therapy. For a patient with newly diagnosed nonmetastatic HER2-positive cancer, what features would make you lean towards surgery?

Kruse: Yeah, this is also a big topic of conversation when we first meet a patient, because I think without the HER2 knowledge, many of them come in assuming they're just going to go to surgery first because that's what happens for the vast majority of patients with breast cancer, early-stage breast cancer. So I try to explain to them that when HER2 is positive, it gives us the opportunity to give treatments before surgery to help understand how effective those treatments are.

So usually in our guidelines, we use about a 2-cm tumor as a cutoff for how large a cancer in the breast has to be to consider that preoperative chemotherapy. And any lymph node positivity generally also moves a patient into that group where we would use systemic therapy before surgery or neoadjuvant therapy, whereas the smaller tumors and negative lymph nodes, typically we would think about going to surgery first. And the reason for that really is that the intensity of the systemic therapy that we give is vastly different if you do it before surgery versus after surgery.

Mangels: What about if there is a bit of a gray area in terms of which way to go?

Kruse: Yeah, so those are our T1cN0 patients more commonly. These are tumors that are bigger than a centimeter, but less than 2 cm and node negative clinically. Those are our most challenging situations because we want to be able to personalize and adapt the systemic therapy as much as possible. And the best way to do that is to give neoadjuvant therapy, but you worry that you're being too heavy handed if you're giving these neoadjuvant regimens to patients with those smaller tumors.

And so many times I will lay that out with a patient and say, "Hey, there is some gray zone here. Here's the pluses, here's the minuses. Here's what duration of treatment would look like." Some patients really can't imagine going through 4 to 6 months of treatment with a tumor still in their body. And if that's the case and we know that we're going to make their quality of life much worse by trying to do this, maybe that pushes us one way.

These are also the great cases for tumor board again, where you say, "Hey," to your breast surgeon, "How easy do you think the surgery's going to be in the current state? Do you need me to try to shrink this tumor? Does that lymph node really look negative?" So in the gray zone cases, again, you're putting the puzzle pieces together to figure out what's the best way forward. And at the end of the day, sometimes you just have to say, "This is what my gut tells me and we're going to go with it." And most patients actually really appreciate that and they'll say, "Whatever you think is best, we should just do it."

Mangels: When neoadjuvant therapy is indicated, you as a clinician have multiple anti-HER2 agents as options. How do you weigh things like efficacy, maturity of evidence, toxicity, and patient preferences when you're making your choice?

Kruse: Yeah. It's amazing that all of those factors are going through your head at one moment in time.

Kruse: It's quite a juggling act. I would say that I come into a patient's room trying to have thought about all of this already so that I at least have my own mature sense of what I would recommend. Sometimes I go into that room and I learn about the patient and I realize I've got to flex. This plan is not going to work.

But I think when I'm coming up with that optimal plan, the first part of that is weighing largely efficacy and toxicity. When we think about these preoperative regimens in particular, the efficacy in terms of getting rid of all the cancer that you can see at the time of surgery really is our north star -- that's that pathologic complete response data point that we see in a lot of our trials. And the reason that that's so important is that pathologic complete response is an excellent surrogate for overall cancer control, overall survival, living without breast cancer recurrence.

And so when I'm looking at trials, that pathologic complete response data point is really what I'm going for because many of these trials will not have that mature survival data quite yet. But that doesn't mean I wouldn't act on that data. I'm comfortable enough with pCR (pathologic complete response) as an endpoint that we move on that.

But every improvement we've seen in pCR tends to come with some change in the side effect profile. And so that's where you have to think about which side effects are you willing to expose a certain patient to? Can they handle those? Are there long-term effects? And this is where I might view the decisions differently in a younger patient versus an older patient. Am I going to change their day-to-day functioning based on the side effects they develop? And in some of those younger patients, are there long-term consequences that if I cure them of the breast cancer, I may have to deal with a major complication 10, 15 years down the road?

So it really is a balancing act. And especially when it comes to those really long-term complications of treatment, you have to bring those up with your patients early on so that they're fully informed and that they know because some patients wouldn't be willing to take that risk. Even if it's 20% better for their cancer, they may say, "I'm not willing to worry about my heart later on." And we adapt to that.

Mangels: I'm guessing some of your patients are like, "I just want to get this tumor out of me." How do you approach and communicate with those patients that really just want to be done with the cutting part, the tumor excision part?

Kruse: Yeah. If those patients are in the gray zone based on their clinical staging, I would say we respect that decision and we may go to surgery right away. And it may change what their postsurgical systemic therapy looks like, but we still have great options. So if that is really a priority for patients, we honor that.

If there's a patient that has a larger tumor, has positive lymph nodes where I really think that neoadjuvant therapy will be important to them, I try to be as clear as possible as to why we're recommending it. And I think patients will often not realize that as we're treating with the systemic therapy that we are expecting the tumor to shrink and potentially go away. A lot of them worry that we're just getting the treatment in because we want to clear out the blood. It's really interesting that the perceptions of what chemotherapy and HER2-targeted therapy do can be all over the place when patients first come to our office.

But as you talk through that you may see this tumor shrink in real time, you may see your breasts go back to normal if it's heavier or firmer when you start treatment. And when that does happen and patients see that working, there's nothing better. They really believe in the treatment. And so being clear about what the goals are can really help with that conversation.

Mangels: It's also a learning opportunity for you as a clinician. You're seeing how that tumor responds to treatment, which is going to inform what you do going forward.

Kruse: Yeah, that's what it's all about actually. It's like an in-real-time experiment, of course an experiment that we have really excellent reasons to do. I largely tell patients that I want to know how well this treatment works on the tumor, and the only time I'm able to do that is if we still have the tumor in the breast or in the lymph nodes where we can physically feel it or see it on imaging.

Once it's cut out, we're relying on these drugs to work, but we don't really have a direct way to measure how well they're working. And actually that really resonates with patients because a lot of them want to know, did the treatment work or not? And then the counterpoint to that is if the treatment doesn't work, as disappointed as that makes all of us, it gives us an opportunity to flex after surgery and say, OK, we can use something different and try to clean up whatever may not have been killed off by the first wave of therapy.

Mangels: At the lower-risk end in patients, for example, with small node-negative tumors, how do you decide how much chemotherapy and HER2-directed therapy is adequate?

Kruse: It's a really interesting time because we're both deescalating for these low-risk patients and escalating for the higher-risk patients all at the same time. And so we're getting newer trials for these low-risk patients on a very frequent basis actually, where we're trying to remove the chemotherapy, where we're trying to lessen the number of doses of chemotherapy we're giving if we really still believe that we have to give it.

And there also are some approaches that we're using different imaging techniques to try to get a sense of really early response and escalating treatment if we're not seeing that early sign of response and then keeping the treatment lower intensity if we are seeing signs of response.

Mangels: So is that really the deciding factor for deescalation or not?

Kruse: Yeah, for the most part. If you have a lower-risk or medium-risk patient where you're still using preoperative therapy, you may see the early response as a sort of fork in the road of how intense you are with your treatment.

For those really low-risk patients where we've decided we're going to surgery first and then we're giving all of the systemic therapy after surgery, there we have a few different trial options where we can think about which particular type of chemotherapy may we want to use. Right now the conventional is HER2-targeted therapy with about 3 months of chemotherapy and then that HER2-targeted therapy continues on for the remainder of a year.

But there are some trials where we're looking at using different types of HER2-targeted therapy for various periods of time within that year to maybe have a more tolerable experience but still be really effective against the cancer.

Mangels: Are patients surprised to learn sometimes that chemotherapy doesn't have to be a part of the treatment plan?

Kruse: Absolutely, yes. And I think that...

Mangels: Surprised in a good way, I guess.

Kruse: Surprised in a good way, yeah. And we also have to do a lot of breaking down of what do these drugs actually do? What is chemotherapy? What is targeted therapy? Because many patients will assume that anything that goes in through the IV is chemo. And of course, some of our targeted therapies go through the IV, but they're not chemo and they have very different consequences for side effects, risk, how long the infusions are. And so that's a huge part of the education that we do upfront with patients.

Mangels: Chemotherapy is a familiar term with a lot of patients. Surgery, obviously people understand that, but we're talking about things like monoclonal antibodies, TKIs [tyrosine kinase inhibitors], antibody-drug conjugates. How do you explain those concepts in a way that is meaningful to patients? And do patients want to know the details of what those are or not?

Kruse: Yes, patients definitely want to know. Some are like, "OK, just give me what you think is best." But I would say most patients are wondering what the individual components of their treatment are.

Kruse: And what they do and what that means for what they can expect, or if they run into complications, which one of these are really crucial, which ones might be able to be modified or dropped. And so I typically will start with going back to that idea of HER2 being our target and which of these drugs directly go against HER2, and then which of the drugs, like chemotherapy, might affect both HER2-positive cells and general cells of the body. And that's a pretty familiar concept, like what is more specific to the cancer and what might affect my whole body.

And then when it gets into the different types of HER2-targeted medicines, monoclonal antibodies versus TKIs, monoclonal antibodies are generally IV. TKIs are generally oral. So that's kind of a nice split to explain. I don't often get into where in the cells these drugs work.

Mangels: What the effect on the receptor is.

Kruse: Right. Right. Some patients will ask that, so I'm prepared to give that information if they want it, but most patients are satisfied by saying, "OK, this is my HER2-targeted drug."

Occasionally it comes up though where you might think about using monoclonal antibodies upfront, and then if you don't have a great response, you might bring around a TKI later. And there I do find telling patients like, "Hey, this is how it works differently. One of these drugs might be more successful getting to other parts of your body, like the brain, that others would not." And actually that does resonate with them, because then they see it as, "OK, this is a way that you're helping me take care of my whole body in different ways."

Mangels: You alluded to this earlier. How do your patients' lifestyles, support systems, socioeconomic status, how do those affect the treatment decisions that you make?

Kruse: Yeah, it's huge because the best treatment plan only works if the patient's actually able to receive it and able to receive it can be so many things. It can be getting the time off of work to be able to make it to the center, having a ride to get there, having the access to supportive medications like anti-nausea medications if copays are not too high.

So I'm very fortunate that I work within a team that has multiple different providers with different levels of expertise and we can each take our part in this. So my nurse may work on one aspect of what a patient's day-to-day life is like and filling in gaps where they may not have the support at home, but maybe we have resources. Our pharmacist helps in that way as well. And our social workers are really key team members for if we can support patients during this treatment journey with different resources.

Sometimes it's education, sometimes it's personnel support like home nursing. A lot of times it's logistics, like the rides to the center. But sometimes we really do have to adjust our plans to fit whatever a patient's individual circumstances...

Mangels: I was just going to ask you, are there cases where a patient's life situation just precludes doing what you initially thought you would be doing in terms of treatment?

Kruse: Absolutely. And in those situations, you try to be creative. You try to get them the best available medication that's going to be able to fit into that lifestyle. And again, it's different for everyone. And thankfully, as the advances in the field have happened, we have more and more options that allow us to create combinations. There's a ton of data in breast cancer where we can make sure that what we're thinking about doing in a creative way is also safe. That's a huge priority, but you do have to sometimes put your thinking cap on and say, "How might we approach this?"

And again, this is a space where I rely on colleagues, where I'll present cases at tumor board because sometimes you have your blinders on and you need that fresh perspective to say, "Have you considered doing it this way?" And that's very valuable because at the end of the day, we just want to do what's best for the patients.

Mangels: Thanks so much for your insights, Dr. Kruse. And thank you for joining us on "Beyond Diagnosis," where we explore not just what physicians know, but how to effectively and compassionately share that knowledge with patients. See you next time.

#5760. U.S. Acura Dealers Are Now Selling 3,000 Factory Reproduction Parts For Your OG NSX

News about Honda making and selling new reproduction parts for the first-generation NSX has been brewing for more than a year now, but it's finally, actually here. The Honda Heritage Parts program launched in Japan back in April but is now making its way stateside. The automaker announced Monday that more than 3,000 Genuine Honda Reproduction Parts for its first-ever supercar are now available for purchase at Acura dealerships across the U.S. and via the online Honda DreamShop. There are apparently plans for "future expansion" of the program, as well.

The American Honda Motor Co. hasn't released a master list of all 3,000 parts being offered, but taking a quick gander at the program's Japanese webpage shows a wide range of stuff available. You can get a camshaft for the yen equivalent of about $850, an accelerator pedal assembly costs $340, and the car's entire V6 cylinder block can be had for around $6,300. If you're a fan looking for some merch-type items, a little armrest emblem that says "NSX DOHC VTEC" on it and the Japanese NSX owner's manual go for about $40 and $60, respectively.

The O.G. NSX (known to Honda nerds as the NA1 and NA2) was branded in America as an Acura and was sold from model years 1991 to 2005, and the newly produced parts apply to NSXs across that entire production run. The program is called Honda Heritage Parts, by the way, not Honda NSX Heritage Parts, which means reproduced parts for other classic Hondas are almost certainly coming in the future.

From Acura's press release: "Honda Heritage Parts was created to help our customers enjoy their classic Acura and Honda performance models, and it's appropriate that we begin with an iconic model like the first-generation Acura NSX," said American Honda executive vice president Mamadou Diallo (though the emphasis is mine). As the owner of a 2004 S2000 that could definitely use some rejuvenation here and there, hopefully that's the next Honda to get the Heritage Parts treatment.

#5759. This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans

People living thousands of miles apart have reported an extraordinarily strange experience after eating certain wild mushrooms. They begin seeing tiny human figures that appear to move through the real world, walking around objects, climbing over surfaces, and interacting with their surroundings.

These visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, named after the miniature inhabitants of "Gulliver's Travels," who stand just 6 inches tall. For decades, researchers suspected that cultural beliefs and folklore might explain why people in different regions described such similar experiences.

Now, a new study provides evidence that the phenomenon has a biological explanation.

Researchers at the University of Utah (U) used DNA sequencing to identify Lanmaoa asiatica as the mushroom responsible for these unusual hallucinations in Southwest China and the northern Philippines. Surprisingly, their investigation found no evidence of any known psychoactive mushroom compounds, including psilocybin.

The findings suggest that the mushroom may produce an entirely unfamiliar hallucinogenic substance. Identifying that chemical could help scientists better understand neurological disorders, unusual visual experiences, and the processes through which the brain creates our perception of reality.

The research was conducted by Colin Domnauer, a doctoral student at the U, and Bryn Dentinger, a mycologist affiliated with the university and the Natural History Museum of Utah. Their findings were published in the journal Mycologia.

In an interview with @theU, Domnauer explained how researchers traced the mushroom's identity, what makes its effects so unusual, and why the discovery could have implications far beyond the study of fungi.

A Century-Old Mystery of Tiny Human Hallucinations

The scientific mystery dates back to 1934, when Western researchers learned that people in Papua New Guinea sometimes experienced vivid visions of miniature humans after eating wild mushrooms. The bizarre effect became known as "mushroom madness."

During the 1950s and 1960s, anthropologists and mushroom specialists traveled to Papua New Guinea to investigate. Their work pointed toward several possible species belonging to the Boletaceae (bolete) family.

However, chemical testing failed to reveal any substances that could explain the hallucinations. Samples were even examined by Albert Hofmann, the scientist who first isolated psilocybin and discovered LSD. He, too, was unable to identify an active ingredient.

With no chemical explanation available, some researchers began questioning whether the mushrooms were responsible at all. They suggested that the visions might instead arise from cultural expectations or traditional beliefs. By the end of the 1960s, scientific investigation of the phenomenon had largely stopped.

The mystery resurfaced during the 1990s, when people in Yunnan, Southwest China, reported similar hallucinations after eating bolete mushrooms. Although the precise species remained uncertain, researchers suspected a recently described mushroom called Lanmaoa asiatica.

Scientists Identify the Mushroom Behind the Strange Visions

Another important clue appeared in 2024, when Domnauer learned of comparable experiences among an Indigenous community in the remote Northern Cordillera region of the Philippines.

Community members described a wild edible mushroom called "Sedesdem" that could sometimes cause people to see miniature human figures. Similar mushrooms were known locally as "Nonda" in Papua New Guinea and "Jian shou qing" in Yunnan.

These mushrooms have an important place in local food traditions, but consuming them without thoroughly cooking them can trigger the unusual hallucinations.

The Philippine accounts represented a third independent report of wild mushrooms causing remarkably similar visions of tiny people.

To investigate, Domnauer traveled to Yunnan and the Philippines, interviewed local residents, and collected specimens of L. asiatica along with other mushrooms belonging to the Lanmaoa genus.

The fieldwork included the first scientific survey of fungi in the northern Philippines. Researchers then analyzed DNA from the collected mushrooms to establish their identities and evolutionary relationships.

The results revealed that the mushrooms called Jian shou qing in China and Sedesdem in the Philippines were both L. asiatica.

This was an unexpected finding because scientists had previously believed the species occurred only in China.

Dentinger also visited Papua New Guinea in hopes of collecting specimens from the location where the mystery originally began. Unfortunately, unusually dry weather made it impossible to obtain samples for genetic comparison.

Although the Papua New Guinea mushroom remains unverified, the evidence from China and the Philippines provides a compelling connection. Three geographically separated cultures have described the same highly specific hallucinations, and DNA testing has linked two of those cases to a single mushroom species.

That consistency strongly suggests a shared chemical and neurological explanation rather than unrelated cultural influences.

Hallucinations of Tiny Humans That Seem Remarkably Real

What makes these hallucinations especially unusual is their striking similarity across different accounts.

People typically describe seeing dozens or even hundreds of miniature figures, generally measuring between 3 and 30 centimeters tall. The figures appear with extraordinary clarity, often seeming as solid and convincing as actual people.

According to Domnauer, approximately 90% of those experiencing the visions describe figures resembling elves, clowns, or other fairy-like characters, often wearing brightly colored clothing.

Even more surprising is the way these imaginary figures seem to behave.

Rather than floating through walls or ignoring their surroundings, they appear to follow familiar physical rules. They walk around obstacles, move across ordinary objects, and sometimes tumble from the edges of tables.

Domnauer recalled one particularly unusual account involving someone eating soup. The person reported seeing tiny humans leap from a spoon into the bowl, where they began swimming. When the person took another spoonful, the miniature figures reportedly remained visible inside their mouth.

Such detailed interactions distinguish these visions from many other forms of drug-induced hallucination.

A Mysterious Psychedelic Compound Unlike Any Known Drug

Scientists also investigated whether L. asiatica contains any of the chemicals already known to cause psychedelic experiences.

Using both chemical testing and genetic analysis, the researchers searched for established psychoactive compounds found in other mushroom species.

The absence of familiar hallucinogens was particularly intriguing because the mushroom's effects differ so dramatically from those associated with known psychedelic drugs.

Researchers now suspect that L. asiatica produces an unidentified psychoactive substance responsible for the tiny human hallucinations.

The compound has not yet been isolated or chemically identified, so its exact nature and mechanism remain unknown.

Discovering it could open an entirely new avenue of research into how certain chemicals alter visual perception.

What the Mushroom Could Reveal About the Human Brain

Although L. asiatica provides an unusually consistent trigger for Lilliputian hallucinations, the phenomenon is not limited to mushroom consumption.

Stories involving miniature humanlike beings appear throughout folklore around the world. Similar hallucinations have also been documented in people experiencing alcohol withdrawal, dementia, macular degeneration, and other neurological conditions.

These connections suggest that the visions may arise from a fundamental feature of the way the human brain processes visual information.

However, scientists still do not fully understand the neurological mechanisms responsible for these experiences or how best to treat them when they occur in medical settings.

This is where the mysterious mushroom could become especially valuable.

Unlike the neurological and medical conditions in which Lilliputian hallucinations occur relatively rarely, L. asiatica can produce the phenomenon in a more consistent and recognizable way.

If researchers can isolate the chemical responsible, they may gain a useful tool for investigating the brain circuits and processes that create these unusually detailed visual experiences.

Such research could eventually improve scientific understanding of hallucinations associated with neurological diseases.

The research team's next major objective is to isolate and identify the suspected psychedelic compound.

DNA Sequencing Reveals Four Previously Unknown Mushroom Species

The investigation also produced important discoveries about fungal biodiversity.

Rather than studying L. asiatica alone, Domnauer and Dentinger conducted the first comprehensive genomic analysis of the Lanmaoa genus.

They examined 53 mushroom specimens collected from natural habitats and preserved in fungarium collections around the world.

Genetic sequencing revealed 17 species within the group, including four species previously unknown to science.

Remarkably, two of those newly identified species had already been preserved in existing collections in the United States. Their distinct identities had gone unrecognized until researchers examined their DNA.

The analysis also indicated that L. asiatica is the only species in the genus currently known to produce psychoactive effects.

Scientists are now working to reconstruct the group's evolutionary history. They hope to determine how the unusual chemical trait developed and whether closely related mushrooms might produce comparable substances.

The findings also demonstrate the scientific value of museum collections. Specimens preserved for years can contain biological discoveries that become apparent only when newer analytical techniques are applied.

For Domnauer, the hidden diversity found in these collections is a reminder that many species and potentially important biological characteristics remain undiscovered, even among organisms that scientists have already collected.

Exploring Fungi Could Lead to New Medicines and Discoveries

The broader implications extend well beyond unusual hallucinations.

Fungi remain one of the least thoroughly explored groups of organisms, and researchers believe their chemical diversity could provide valuable clues about biology, medicine, and the nervous system.

One of the most famous examples is penicillin, the antibiotic originally obtained from a fungus that transformed the treatment of bacterial infections and became one of the most consequential medical discoveries of the last century.

Scientists hope continued exploration of fungal biodiversity could reveal other medically useful compounds and previously unknown biological processes.

The mysterious effects of L. asiatica illustrate just how much remains to be learned about the fungal kingdom. A mushroom long consumed by communities in Asia may contain a substance capable of revealing new information about the human brain and how it creates conscious experience.

The research received funding from the National Science Foundation (award #DEB-2114785).

Materials provided by University of Utah. Original written by Lisa Potter. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5758. CVS Health plans to split pharmacy business from Aetna, Caremark

CVS Health plans to split pharmacy business from Aetna, Caremark" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The healthcare giant announced Wednesday morning that it would divide its business units into two companies. The first houses its retail pharmacies and Health 100 technology businesses, and will operate as CVS Pharmacy. The second includes Aetna, Caremark, Oak Street Health and Signify Health and will be referred to as CVS Health on an interim basis.

CVS said in the announcement that it expects the separation to be completed in the first half of 2028, subject to closing conditions, and until then, it will continue to operate jointly. The move will reverse CVS' historic acquisition of Aetna for $69 billion in 2018.

Current CVS CEO David Joyner will become chief executive of the new CVS Health, while Prem Shah, group president of CVS Health, will become the CEO of the new CVS Pharmacy unit.

The company said that the decision "follows a comprehensive strategic review" by its board of directors.

Joyner said during the company's earnings call Wednesday morning that the shift comes "from a position of strength" after multiple years of hard work at CVS to shift its strategic approach and drive improvement. That includes significant investments in technology across the enterprise, and an overhaul of its leadership team to drive needed change.

He said that the "environment around us is constantly changing" as the company pushes toward this new strategy.

"We can take this strategic action today because of our tremendous progress since 2024," Joyner said.

"We will be better positioned to address this changing environment as two strong independent healthcare leaders," he continued. "Following a thoughtful and deliberate strategic review by the board and senior management, we have a structure and plan that are built to win and represent the best path to create value over the long term."

During this process, the team has identified significant opportunities for greater integration between Aetna and Caremark and has leaned on those to support key strategic initiatives, like advancing value-based care, Joyner noted. However, the pharmacy business has generally "operated behind a firewall."

"It has always been an arm's length negotiation and structure, which again, just reinforces the fact that there are integration opportunities, but nothing that we cannot solve for with a commercial agreement," Joyner said.

While there are clear synergies that exist between the pharmacies and Caremark, those commercial deals can maintain what's working, he added.

"We don't need the integration in an operating structure," Joyner said. "We need to make sure that we're aligned around where we believe that there can be value creation and make sure that there's an appropriate commercial agreement in place to support that."

CVS' strategy over the past several years has been built on four key principles: delivering on best-in-class execution, rethinking the consumer experience, becoming a go-to partner and harnessing capabilities across the company.

Following the split, both companies will continue to lean on these concepts, CVS said. Each individual entity will also benefit from a more focused strategy and the ability to adapt more nimbly to its own unique goals and strategic needs.

The future CVS Pharmacy will continue to identify ways to expand the reach of its pharmacists and identify further partnerships across the healthcare spectrum, while CVS Health will adapt in new ways to serve its clients, the company said.

Joyner said the company will continue to be transparent about its progress during the separation process.

Shares in the company were up 3% pre-market as of about 7:30 a.m. ET. CVS also reported its Q3 earnings on Wednesday, posting $2.2 billion in profit and $108.4 billion in revenue for the quarter.

Joyner said on the earnings call that post-split, investors will own shares in both companies.

#5757. Suzuki GSX-10R And SV-7S Put New Twists On Old Classics

Suzuki has long been, for better and for worse, a motorcycle maker that keeps its old assembly lines running. While the company comes up with something truly new every once in a while, it's more likely to figure out a new combination of parts it already has laying around. So, for EICMA, we shouldn't be surprised that Suzuki's big announcements are based around engines old enough to drink. We also shouldn't be surprised that those engines are inside what look to be some damn good bikes.

Suzuki's big reveals this year are the SV-7S and GSX-10R, bikes built around the 27-year-old SV650 engine and 21-year-old K5 GSX-R1000 engines, respectively. The former looks to be a mild update to the outgoing SV650, with new lighting, emissions equipment, a quickshifter, and a ride-by-wire throttle wrapped around the prior bike's frame and engine. Most importantly, the SV-7S is available in Europe, meaning that the 645 cc V-twin lives on under Euro 5+ emissions. Suzuki's site doesn't list power claims for the new bike, but it's likely to make the same 73 horses it has since time immemorial.

While the SV-7S is an update and a name change for the SV650, the GSX-10R (above) is ostensibly an entirely new bike — admittedly a bike that's largely just a faired version of the GSX-S1000, the company's naked literbike. #5755. Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch

A new analysis from Monash University suggests that low-dose aspirin may be linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia in older adults with certain genetic characteristics. Researchers found that people with a specific genetic profile who took aspirin had a 70 percent lower relative risk of developing dementia, raising the possibility that genetic testing could eventually help identify people who might benefit from preventive treatments.

The findings, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, were based on genetic data from more than 13,500 participants in the landmark ASPREE Trial (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly). Scientists examined whether differences in participants' genes could help explain why aspirin might affect dementia risk differently from one person to another.

Aspirin Linked to 70% Lower Dementia Risk in Certain People

The most striking results involved genes associated with platelet count. Platelets are small components of the blood that help form clots, and researchers wanted to determine whether genetic variations related to platelet levels could influence aspirin's potential effects on dementia.

After assigning participants genetic scores associated with platelet count, the team compared dementia rates among those who received aspirin and those given a placebo.

Among people in the highest 20 percent of platelet count genetic scores, just 1 percent of aspirin users developed dementia, compared with 3.3 percent of participants taking a placebo. That difference translates to approximately a 70 percent lower relative risk of dementia among those receiving aspirin.

However, the apparent benefit was accompanied by a significant safety concern. In the same genetic group, 4.4 percent of aspirin users experienced major bleeding, compared with 2.1 percent of those receiving a placebo.

A Genetic Clue Could Change Dementia Prevention

Lead author Dr. Peter Fransquet, a Research Fellow at Monash's School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said the results suggest that a person's genetic makeup could eventually play an important role in determining which dementia prevention strategies are most appropriate.

"Previous trials found aspirin didn't prevent dementia when everyone was considered together," Dr. Fransquet said.

"Our findings suggest there may be more to the story.

"In people with this particular genetic profile, we saw substantially fewer cases of dementia among those taking aspirin.

"It raises the possibility that genetics could one day help us identify who may benefit from a preventive treatment, rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach."

The possibility of more targeted prevention is especially important as dementia becomes increasingly common. Dementia Australia estimates that approximately 446,500 people in Australia are living with the condition in 2026. That number is expected to exceed one million by 2065.

Blood Platelets Reveal an Unexpected Dementia Connection

Previous research has connected dementia with platelet activation and aggregation, the processes through which platelets become active and stick together. However, scientists have had a less complete understanding of how a person's overall platelet count might relate to dementia.

The new findings point toward platelet biology as a potentially important area of investigation. Notably, the genetic association identified by researchers did not involve the well-established genetic risk factors typically linked to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.

"What's particularly interesting is that the signal wasn't linked to the established genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease and dementia," Dr. Fransquet said.

"Instead, it's pointing us towards platelet biology and gives us a new avenue to investigate."

Why More Research Is Needed Before Taking Aspirin

Although the findings suggest that aspirin could have different effects depending on a person's genes, researchers emphasize that the results must be confirmed before they can guide medical recommendations.

The next step is to investigate whether the association appears in other populations. Scientists would then need to conduct a clinical trial specifically involving people with the genetic profile identified in the analysis.

"We now need to confirm the finding in other studies and ultimately test it in a trial designed specifically for people with this genetic profile.

"People shouldn't start taking aspirin to prevent dementia on the basis of this study without consulting with their doctor, particularly given the increased risk of serious bleeding.

"If it holds up, the fact that aspirin is already cheap and widely available could make personalized dementia prevention a real possibility."

Materials provided by Monash University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Waystar touts bigger health system wins and growing AI pipeline" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare payment software maker Waystar again outperformed analysts’ estimates in the third quarter as the company builds out new artificial intelligence capabilities and drives growth by adding new customers and selling more of its platform to existing clients.

Waystar brought in $325.6 million in Q3 revenue, up 21% from the same period a year ago, according to its Q3 financial results published Monday afternoon. It beat Wall Street analysts’ estimates by 0.46%.

During Q3, the company reported $181 million in subscription revenue, up 34%, while provider revenue grew 28% to reach $243 million. Patient revenue came in at $82 million, up 5% year-over-year, and volume-based revenue grew 8% to $143 million.

Waystar ended the quarter with 1,488 clients generating more than $100,000 of trailing 12-month revenue, up 14% year-over-year. Year-to-date bookings grew 25% year-over-year.

Waystar reported net income of $31 million and GAAP net income per share of 16 cents. It also reported adjusted EBITDA of $139.3 million and non-GAAP earnings per share of 44 cents.

Waystar provides healthcare payment and revenue cycle management tools to 30,000 clients, representing over 1.5 million distinct providers. Its platform processes over 8.5 billion healthcare payment transactions annually, representing more than $3 trillion in gross claims, according to CEO Matt Hawkins. Waystar says its clinical intelligence spans approximately one-third of U.S. hospital discharges. In 2026, Waystar added more than 100 direct connections to health plans, supporting nearly 50 million transactions annually, executives said.

Hawkins told investors and analysts during the Q3 earnings call that the quarter “reflects strong progress,” on three strategic priorities of “driving broader adoption of the Waystar platform, extending our reach through partners and integrations, and advancing AI and innovation.”

“Our near-term roadmap includes more than 20 planned AI capabilities, accelerating the autonomous revenue cycle vision to reduce manual work, automate increasingly complex tasks and improve financial and operational outcomes for our clients,” Hawkins said.

Waystar is focused on using AI to reshape the RCM process with a vision of building an "autonomous revenue cycle" that can reduce manual work, automate increasingly complex tasks and improve financial and operational outcomes for healthcare organizations, executives said.

In Q3, Waystar launched an autonomous claim resubmission capability that interprets payer responses, applies payer-specific intelligence to determine the next action and autonomously resubmits eligible rejected claims with minimal human intervention, Hawkins said.

"Based on early adopter results and the initial claim types supported, we estimate this capability could autonomously resubmit up to $5 billion in previously rejected claims annually with the potential to eliminate more than 400,000 hours of manual work each year," he said.

The company is also targeting mid-cycle processes. "We're combining Waystar's financial data, payer intelligence, workflows and connectivity with Iodine's clinical intelligence to bring greater automation earlier in the revenue cycle," Hawkins noted.

The company acquired AI-driven RCM company Iodine Software a year ago to add its clinical intelligence capabilities to Waystar's software. Iodine bookings exceeded management's year-to-date plan by 74% in Q3, Hawkins said. Iodine's CDI and pre-bill anomaly detection products generated nearly $30 million in bookings through Q3, including about $15 million during the quarter, and have a combined pipeline exceeding $100 million.

The company is winning bigger, broader deals in the healthcare market, Hawkins asserted. Large health care organizations increasingly look to Waystar to support more of the revenue cycle through a single connected platform, he said on the call. "Within our large client cohort, which we define as clients generating more than $100,000 in LTM revenue, the average client now uses approximately five Waystar product modules. With over 30 modules across six product families, we see significant opportunity to continue driving broader platform adoption within these relationships," he said.

Hawkins added that the company “secured the largest new client win in Waystar’s history” during Q3.

“In a competitive process, a major East Coast health system representing approximately $7 billion in annual net patient revenue selected Waystar's full platform across patient access, mid-cycle, and back-end revenue cycle operations,” he said. “The organization plans to replace more than 20 separate vendors with Waystar as it simplifies its technology infrastructure and streamlines operations.”

Moreover, Hawkins said the company is expanding its reach with “strategic channel relationships,” with an emphasis on the ambulatory market—noting an expanded partnership with a leading physical therapy practice management system that expands Waystar’s reach to “nearly 4,000 providers across more than 2,500 sites, representing approximately 17 million claims annually.”

“Decisions like these reflect the trust we've built with channel partners, the breadth of our platform, and our ability to deliver real ROI,” Hawkins said.

Alpana Wegner, who took over as Waystar’s chief financial officer in August, said that large client relationships “now represent approximately 75% of revenue,” adding the company is seeing momentum across growth in number of clients, strong bookings and implementation backlog expansion.

But larger, broader platform implementations have longer revenue conversion times, which can extend to 12 to 18 months, Wegner noted. This creates a longer period between booking and recognized revenue. The company reported that the backlog of larger deals, those in excess of $100,000 in annual sales, was up more than 50% year-over-year.

In response to a question from an analyst about the disconnect between bookings and revenue growth, Hawkins said, "We are seeing strong demand. We're not seeing a change in the competitive environment or our win rates, and we're pleased with that," adding that the company sees a "long-term double-digit opportunity to drive revenue."

For its full-year outlook, Waystar management forecasted revenue of $1.277 billion to $1.287 billion, with a midpoint of $1.282 billion. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be between $543 million and $549 million for fiscal 2026.

The company expects slower, near-term revenue growth, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $323 million, representing growth of about 6%.

Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote in an analyst note that Waystar delivered strong results on both the top and bottom line. "We continue to expect solid organic growth going forward. While investor focus may turn to the very modest (0.2%) reduction in sales guidance, we believe strong profitability, solid bookings performance, and robust free cash flows will continue to lead the stock higher over time; we maintain our Outperform rating," he wrote.

Daniels wrote that Waystar remains a "category leader in end-to-end RCM software... leveraging its competitive position and scale advantages to enhance the platform with innovations that drive client value. Moreover, we believe innovation momentum is driving an uptick in pipeline activity, size, and bookings performance, highlighted by a continuation of strong win rates and an uptick in larger deal sizes."

Daniels also noted that concerns over AI risks and "end-market noise," such as weaker healthcare volumes and Medicaid and ACA exchange lives moving to uninsured status, are "overblown."

Waystar is positioned to capitalize on the AI-enabled transformation of RCM via stronger pricing, an expanding total addressable market and increased value-add for clients, he said. "We continue to view the sales model as highly recurring (and visible) and do not anticipate any major AI-related competitive disruption as providers continue to turn toward trusted and fully integrated partners for RCM solutions," Daniels wrote.

#5753. Child Dies of Measles in Wisconsin's First Such Death Since 1990

— Four measles-associated deaths confirmed by CDC this year, but states report higher numbers

An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the state's first death from the disease in 36 years, state officials announced Thursday.

The coroner listed the cause of death as measles, state health officials said.

"My heart is broken for the family," said Kirsten Johnson, MPH, secretary of the state health department. "Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease."

The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.

The CDC has confirmed four measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. In Pennsylvania alone, health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.

As of Thursday, Wisconsin reported 431 cases of measles, all but three in unvaccinated people. Nine people had been hospitalized.

#5752. Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication

Missing doses of blood pressure medication could significantly reduce its ability to protect against heart attacks, strokes, and other serious cardiovascular problems, according to findings presented at ESC Congress 2026.

An estimated 1.4 billion adults worldwide between the ages of 30 and 79 have high blood pressure (hypertension), a major contributor to illness and death. Although medications that lower blood pressure are proven to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications, approximately half of patients do not take their prescriptions as directed.

"We have evidence that poor adherence to antihypertensive medication is associated with worse outcomes," explained presenter, Miss Qianqian Yang from the University of Oxford, UK. "However, previous data has come from observational studies and could be confounded by other factors. We undertook an analysis of randomized trial data to assess the true impact of adherence on the benefits of antihypertensive treatment."

Major Study Examines the Impact of Missed Blood Pressure Medication

To better understand how consistently taking medication affects its benefits, researchers analyzed individual patient data from 91,339 participants across nine clinical trials. Each trial compared a blood pressure treatment (intervention group) with an alternative approach (comparator group: either placebo or a less-intensive regimen).

The researchers divided participants into two categories based on how closely they followed their prescribed treatment. Those who took at least 80% of their assigned medication were considered to have higher adherence, while those who took less than 80% were placed in the lower adherence group.

Even with the regular monitoring and structured conditions of clinical trials, patients became less consistent about taking their medication as time passed.

"A decline in adherence over time was apparent, even in the structured setting of trials," noted Miss Yang. Overall, 88% of participants met the higher adherence threshold during the first year, but that figure had dropped to just 79% by the fifth year.

Skipping Blood Pressure Pills Reduces Treatment Benefits

The difference in medication adherence was reflected in how much patients' blood pressure improved.

Among participants with higher adherence, systolic blood pressure, the top number in a blood pressure reading, was 5.2 mmHg lower in the intervention group than in the comparator group. For those with lower adherence, the difference was considerably smaller at just 3.0 mmHg.

Researchers then examined whether these differences translated into protection against major cardiovascular problems. The outcomes included strokes, heart attacks (myocardial infarction), ischemic heart disease, and heart failure that resulted in hospitalization or death.

The findings revealed a striking contrast. Among patients who consistently followed their treatment plans, the intervention group experienced an 11% lower incidence of major cardiovascular events compared with the comparator group. However, among patients with lower adherence, there was no statistically significant reduction in these events.

"Notably, our results reinforce the saying that 'drugs don't work in patients who don't take them.' Patients with lower adherence derived little or no cardiovascular benefit, whereas those with higher adherence had greater reductions in blood pressure and prevention of cardiovascular events," said Miss Yang.

Helping Patients Get Lifesaving Heart Protection

The researchers believe that helping people take their medication consistently should become a greater priority in the treatment of high blood pressure. They recommend more routine assessments of medication adherence, along with better patient education and practical strategies to make treatment easier to follow.

Possible approaches include simplifying medication schedules, combining multiple treatments into a single pill, and prescribing longer-acting drugs that can help limit the consequences of an occasional missed dose.

Professor Felix Mahfoud, Chair of the ESC Communication Committee, emphasized that missed medication has received too little attention as a contributor to poorly controlled blood pressure.

"For years, we have neglected non-adherence to medication as a cause for uncontrolled hypertension. Assessment of adherence should become a routine part of hypertension care so patients do not miss out on life-saving benefits. As healthcare providers, we are here to have open, non-judgmental conversations with our patients about any barriers they may have to taking medication, to help improve adherence."

Materials provided by European Society of Cardiology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5751. What Democratic control of Congress means for healthcare in 2027

What Democratic control of Congress means for healthcare in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Tuesday’s forecast-busting blue wave puts wind in the sails of Democrats who have promised a stark departure from Trump-era healthcare policy—though whether or not the shifts will be incremental or seismic hinges on intra-party debates and the president’s veto.

As of noon Wednesday, Democrats had flipped seven seats in the Senate and 21 in the House, setting the party up for comfortable majorities as unexpected battleground races continue to be tallied.

Healthcare issues were a major talking point through many midterm election campaigns. In battleground Senate races, for instance, Democrats spent $65 million on ads primarily focused on healthcare, more than twice that of their next-most prominent topic. Healthcare was overall the second-most prominent issue featured in ads (as measured by spend) across the two parties, behind a push on taxation topics from Republicans.

And within those ads: promises to deliver lower costs, greater coverage and federal oversight, starting Jan. 1, 2027.

The immediate legislative impact will be seen in the bills new chamber leaders bring to the floor.

A health policy agenda circulated in September by a working group under Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.)—the House’s current minority leader and likely speaker in the next Congress—outlined immediate, “First 100 Hours” goals that include repeal of the Medicaid coverage and funding cuts of 2025’s H.R. 1 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) as well as restoration of enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that expired at the top of 2026 and vastly increased marketplace plan premiums.

Other 100-hours priorities outlined in the document include medical debt protections, removal of visa program fees for healthcare workers, an end to an AI prior authorization program in Traditional Medicare, restoration of withheld National Institutes of Health funding, a block on immigration enforcement operations in hospitals and guaranteed no-cost coverage of recommended vaccines regardless of changes in federal recommendations.

Additionally, the new majorities would install key Democratic policy heads to congressional committees responsible for advancing healthcare legislation and conducting oversight into government and private sector conduct. Among those new chairs would be Vermont’s Bernie Sanders, a vocal opponent of corporate interests in healthcare and the country’s chief Medicare for All advocate, who would chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee; and Oregon’s Ron Wyden, who as Finance Committee ranking member recently pursued oversight of Medicaid stakeholders, endorsed Sanders’ Medicare for All bill, led calls to hold “Big Insurance” accountable for administrative roadblocks to care and summarized his midterms reaction with a single word: “Subpoenas.”

Underpinning the party’s legislative leaders are a slew of new-to-office healthcare advocates. Several of those elected to Congress have backgrounds as physicians or other COVID-era public health experience. Among the standouts are Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton, a pediatrician who was director of the state’s Department of Health and resigned early in the pandemic in protest of state leadership; and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and Detroit’s former health director, who has made progressive health policy goals like Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign.

For the public and the healthcare industry, the key question is how Democrats will pursue their healthcare agenda under a divided government and lame-duck president.

Molly Turco, who covers healthcare policy at TD Cowen Washington Research Group, wrote in a Wednesday policy note that “with Trump in the [White House], passage of major reforms are very unlikely and even medium-sized policies, like rollbacks of Medicaid [state-directed payment] cuts or restoring ACA subsidies, are an uphill battle. But the midterm results and catalysts like the debt ceiling give Ds leverage.”

Consultants at BRG, in a media roundtable late last week, generally agreed with the veto hurdle, but noted that a stymied Congress still has room to write and pass bills that could become new policy in a future majority, as was the case with Medicaid work requirements pushed by Republicans during the end of the Biden administration but ultimately codified last year.

There is still an avenue for dealmaking between the parties, analysts and advisors noted, such as on areas with general bipartisan agreement (think this year’s pharmacy benefit manager reforms, or other major pain points like physician pay or surprise billing arbitration reform) as part of must-pass spending packages slated for this December and the coming years. The president, for his part, told outlets late Tuesday night that he intends to work with Democrats to pass bills he believes will benefit the country—while also highlighting his willingness to veto.

PricewaterhouseCoopers, in a Wednesday policy note, said “targeted bipartisan legislation is most likely to move. Look for action on cybersecurity, AI, price transparency, modernizing drug development and prior authorization processes. Regardless of congressional gridlock, continued regulatory implementation will shape near-term business and compliance requirements.”

Turco’s note predicts a dual messaging strategy for congressional Democrats on affordability and accountability, with the latter involving “an aggressive corporate investigation and hearings strategy.”

The TD Cowen analyst also questioned whether Democrats’ midterm over-performance and gains by progressive candidates will embolden the party to pursue and campaign on “bold” healthcare reforms like Medicare for All ahead of 2028.

Wyden’s recent endorsement of Sanders’ reform bill “is a powerful signal that even long-tenured moderates are under pressure to have a vision that reimagines [healthcare],” Turco wrote, though “many other D members are worried about blowback from M4A support that has almost no chance of being a viable policy. These members are vocal about their concerns and want to work on more realistic policies like restoring the ACA and Medicaid, building on IRA negotiations, reducing premiums/ deductibles for employer-based coverage, adding more benefits to Medicare, etc.”

Investment banking firm William Blair’s equity research team, in an election day brief, noted that Democratic governorships bring immediate impact to the healthcare industry as states make strategic decisions on how to implement, or offset, the provisions of H.R. 1.

The limited avenues for swiftly rolling back that sweeping bill mean that industry players, including Medicare Advantage plans and margin-strapped hospitals, should begin preparing for its financial headwinds, consultants and health systems heads have said. But that doesn’t mean Democrats’ strong night has dashed all hopes for rollbacks or other tweaks to ease the pain.

“While the election has changed who controls Congress, it doesn't change the financial challenges hospitals will face in 2027,” Chris Van Gorder, president and CEO of nonprofit integrated health system Scripps Health, said in a statement reacting to midterm election results. “Democrats won't have the votes to simply reverse major federal health care cuts over a presidential veto. But Congress is far from powerless. Lawmakers can use their oversight and budget authority to press for changes in how those cuts are carried out, protect critical health care funding where possible and work across party lines to ease the growing financial pressures on hospitals and impact on patients."

Even if political gridlock takes hold, Tuesday’s results ensure that affordability will be center stage in Washington, analysts said, especially as consumers’ cost pressures will likely persist well through the 2028 election cycle.

“Even where legislation stalls, don’t dismiss the headlines,” PwC advised healthcare executives. “Democratic hearings, investigations and proposed bills offer insight into the policies taking shape for 2028, while growing pressure around affordability continues to push the healthcare market toward consumer expectations. Executives who look beyond near-term political conflict, plan for multiple policy scenarios and adapt to evolving consumer demands will be better positioned for potential healthcare reform after 2028.”

On the virtual care front, ATA Action, the advocacy-focused affiliate of the American Telemedicine Association, said the election presents an opportunity to build on strong bipartisan support for telehealth and virtual care at the federal and state levels. The group plans to continue working across party lines to make Medicare telehealth policies permanent, expand digital health access and remove regulatory barriers to virtual care, Kyle Zebley, CEO of the ATA and Executive Director of ATA Action, said in a statement.

#5749. Patients Want 'Deep Plane' Facelifts. Are They Actually Better?

— Plastic surgeons weigh in on different rhytidectomy techniques

Welcome to Culture Clinic, MedPage Today's collaboration with Northwell Health to offer a healthcare professional's take on the latest viral medical topics.

As elective plastic surgery procedures, including facelifts, become more popular among everyday Americans, plastic surgeons say more people come in requesting "deep plane" facelifts.

Aviva Preminger, MD, a spokesperson for the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, has experienced this in her own practice in New York City. Whereas historically patients would come in asking for a facelift, now they ask for deep plane facelifts specifically.

"I think that the deep plane facelift is really having a moment right now, especially because of social media," Preminger told MedPage Today.

Indeed, there's been ample speculation online -- including from plastic surgeons -- about Kris Jenner, guessing that she's had a deep plane facelift.

While there's more awareness about deep plane facelifts, there's also some simmering misinformation, Preminger cautioned, noting that "social media can sometimes create the impression that one technique is universally superior for everyone," which isn't the case.

Deep plane facelifts aren't new; the procedure was first described by plastic surgeon Sam Hamra, MD, in 1990. Unlike traditional superficial facelifts, deep plane facelifts go below the superficial musculoaponeurotic system, which is the fibromuscular layer that supports the facial soft tissues.

"By releasing certain retaining ligaments, the surgeon can actually mobilize and reposition the deeper tissues of the cheeks, jawline, and the lower face, with the goal being to restore a more youthful facial contour without placing too much tension on the skin," Preminger said. Essentially, the intent of this procedure is "to address the deeper structural layers of the face rather than simply tightening the skin," she added.

Both traditional and deep plane facelifts involve incisions by the ears and at the hairline, but the exact position depends on skin laxity.

Lyle Leipziger, MD, chief of plastic surgery at Northwell Health's North Shore University Hospital in Manhasset, New York, and Long Island Jewish Medical Center in New Hyde Park, New York, told MedPage Today that deep plane facelifts are most appropriate for the mid-face, but there are a lot of considerations, like skin texture and tone, how a patient looked when they were younger, and how their face has sagged with age.

Because deep plane facelifts involve both tightening and repositioning, the results should be long-lasting. But Leipziger emphasized that one technique isn't superior to the other; it's a matter of choosing the appropriate strategy for a patient's facial structure and aesthetic goals.

Both traditional and deep plane facelifts should have longevity, he noted, but a consultation with an experienced surgeon is vital. That way, the surgeon can have an open conversation with the patient setting realistic expectations.

"You shouldn't choose a facelift based on the name of the technique alone," Leipziger said. "The technique really should be tailored to the face and not the other way around."

Depending on a patient's goals, Preminger said that it's not uncommon for surgeons to combine facelifts with other facial procedures. It used to be the case that patients were told to expect their facelift to last about 10 years, she added, but plastic surgery has improved greatly. Patients' genetics, sun exposure, and weight loss all impact the longevity of results, but patients now have access to non-surgical maintenance, like laser resurfacing, botulinum toxin (Botox), and filler, which add to the procedure's longevity.

Preminger said that facelifts aren't particularly painful, but innovation in the plastic surgery space still makes for better experiences. She noted that tranexamic acid can help reduce bruising, hemostatic nets can help reduce swelling and avoid the use of drains, and suzetrigine (Journavx) is a non-narcotic working well for post-op pain control.

More than anything, this trend reflects a broader cultural shift where plastic surgery is no longer thought of as a luxury only for the rich and famous but as an option for anyone willing to pay for it, surgeons said.

CommonSpirit Health signs definitive agreement to sell 3 more N.D. hospitals to Altru Health System" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

CommonSpirit Health has locked in a deal to sell three hospitals to Altru Health System, a rural North Dakota nonprofit.

The deal is contingent on regulatory review and other customary closing conditions, but is expected to close in early 2027. The pair's new definitive agreement, announced Wednesday, follows 10 months of due diligence following a letter of intent unveiled near the top of the year (see that story below). Financial details were not disclosed.

The to-be-sold facilities are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison.

They would join Altru's flagship acute care hospital, a critical access hospital it also purchased from CommonSpirit in March, a trauma center, a specialty hospital and 20 practices spread across northern North Dakota.

The organizations said there are no changes to patient care or day-to-day operations related to the deal. The hospitals will maintain their Catholic identity and mission.

"Through our work together over the years, we’ve developed tremendous confidence in Altru’s commitment to high-quality, compassionate care," Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health's Central Region, said in reference to prior partnerships with the health system. "We believe Altru is the right partner to build on St. Alexius’ proud legacy, honor its Catholic mission and continue serving patients and families for generations to come.”

CommonSpirit is in the midst of a sweeping operational overhaul as it looks to bolster its financial performance ahead of imminent Medicaid cuts. Those efforts have opened the $42.4 billion system to a string of hospital divestitures, including its four handoffs to Altru as well as the sale of a four-hospital Ohio system to UPMC in September.

CommonSpirit Health and Altru Health System are considering a deal to transfer three North Dakota hospitals to the latter, the organizations announced Thursday.

The pair’s signed letter of intent outlines plans to evaluate a potential deal for the facilities, a process they said would run “the next several months” before a potential definitive agreement might be struck.

In the balance are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison. All three are Catholic facilities within CommonSpirit’s regional healthcare system CHI St. Alexius Health.

Potential financial terms of any deal for the hospitals were not disclosed, nor were any details on whether other assets tied to the hospitals, such as clinics, would be included.

“This is a natural next step in exploring how we can continue to support strong, sustainable healthcare for the region,” Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health’s central region, which includes CHI St. Alexius Health, said in the announcement.

CommonSpirit is a $40 billion nonprofit that counted 137 hospitals in two dozen states. It’s in the midst of an operating performance turnaround initiative and, at this month’s J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference, teased “a couple” of portfolio divestitures to be announced in the next quarter as part of the effort.

Grand Forks, North Dakota-based Altru Health System is a smaller nonprofit, with just over $700 million of revenue in 2024 from its sole acute care hospital, a specialty hospital and 20 practice locations in northeast North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. It opened a new $500 million hospital in January 2025.

The news comes hot on the heels of another deal between the systems for ownership of CHI St. Alexius Health Devils Lake, another critical access hospital. That handoff was unveiled in December and is set to close March 1.

Both deals have been described as a boon for rural communities and an opportunity for Altru to better coordinate its local care.

“Altru has a long history of serving communities across North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, and our organizations share a deep respect for the people we serve and the responsibility that comes with delivering local healthcare,” Todd Forkel, CEO of Altru, said in the announcement. “We look forward to working more closely with CommonSpirit to strengthen access to care for patients and families well into the future.”
